parts: Lesson 8: Language Press in India — Summary

Newspapers in India are English or language (regional) newspapers. Mumbai Samachar, the Gujarati daily published in 1822 from Mumbai, is the oldest existing newspaper. Language papers are published in more than 100 languages (main ones in 16 principal languages; 22 languages are in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution) and reach even interior villages, shaping public opinion.

English papers: published in one language, concentrated in big cities, read by the well-educated middle and upper income groups, little rural penetration, follow the British tradition, earn more advertisement revenue, colourful and flamboyant. Language papers: published in many languages, circulated all over the country including villages, read even by lower-middle class and below, evolved their own style, earn less advertisement revenue and adopt a simple style.

At independence India had 3533 publications (330 dailies, 3203 periodicals); the number grew twelve-fold. India has the world's largest newspaper market after China; the top three countries in circulation are China, India and Japan. Growth is measured by circulation (copies sold) and readership (people reading; one copy may have four or five readers). Readership is higher for language newspapers. Reasons for the newspaper boom: rise in literacy (Robin Jeffrey), expansion of the middle class, untapped market (about 350 million literate non-buyers), education of women, technological advancement (new editions easier), better purchasing power and lower prices, aggressive marketing with gifts and concessions, and political awareness.

Added reasons: rural economy (more than 60 per cent of people live in villages; farmers have become an influential consumer group), prominent coverage of local news (first by southern newspapers), multiple editions from district centres, and the advertising boom aimed at the rural market. Malayala Manorama (started 1890) was the largest circulated daily in the 1980s; Ananda Bazar Patrika was the largest from a single centre; Dainik Jagran and Dainik Bhaskar are today the largest dailies. Between 1998 and 2000 Malayalam, Bengali, Hindi and Marathi grew fastest. Hindi has the largest number of newspapers and circulation; Uttar Pradesh publishes the most newspapers in a single language (Hindi). The National Readership Survey 2006 showed rural readers (110 million) roughly equal to urban (112 million).

The Registrar of Newspapers for India (RNI, set up 1956 on the recommendation of the first Press Commission; minimum circulation of 2000 for government advertisements), the Audit Bureau of Circulation (ABC, a non-government body of publishers and advertisers set up in 1948) and the National Readership Studies Council (NRSC, readership surveys every six months) keep records. Books: Robin Jeffrey's India's Newspaper Revolution, S. Natarajan's A History of Press in India. Publishers submit annual statements under Section 19D of the Press and Registration of Books Act 1867.

Unhealthy trends: predatory price wars (small papers suffer), dependence on advertisements (government ads exceed 50 per cent, limiting criticism), cut-throat competition, media trials, fake sting operations, privacy violations, glamourization of criminals, promoting hatred, mud-slinging and gifts and coupons. Future: the narrowing of the urban and rural divide, rise in literacy, education, industry growth, the new middle class and modern communication systems will increase the circulation of language papers.
